NEUROLOGICAL__Headache:
Headache is common and usually benign, but the job is to screen out the dangerous secondary causes before pattern-matching a primary headache. Take a focused history — onset (sudden vs gradual), time course, triggers/relievers, associated features and age — and run the red flags. A thunderclap onset, fever with neck stiffness, a new headache over 50 with scalp tenderness, or a progressive headache with focal signs or papilloedema each point to a serious cause. If the red flags are clear, sort the primary type: migraine, tension-type or cluster.
🚨Thunderclap (peaks <5 min) → subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise — CT then LP (see intracranial haemorrhage). Fever + neck stiffness + photophobia → meningitis / encephalitis (see meningitis, meningism). New headache >50 with scalp tenderness / jaw claudication → giant cell arteritis — high-dose steroids now to save sight (see GCA / vasculitis). Progressive, worse on waking / lying / coughing, with vomiting, focal signs or papilloedema → raised ICP / space-occupying lesion (see raised ICP, brain tumour).

1Recognise & classify
🔍Take the history & split it
  • Onset: sudden / thunderclap (vascular) vs gradual; time course: acute, episodic, chronic or progressive
  • Associated features: aura, autonomic signs, fever, focal deficit, visual symptoms; and age (new headache >50 is a red flag)
  • First exclude a secondary (dangerous) cause, then match the primary type (migraine / tension / cluster)
🚩Red flags — secondary causes
  • Thunderclap → SAH (also CVST, dissection, pituitary apoplexy) — see intracranial haemorrhage
  • Fever + meningism → meningitis / encephalitis; >50 + scalp tenderness / jaw claudication → GCA (steroids + ESR, see jaw claudication)
  • Progressive + worse on waking / Valsalva + vomiting / focal signs / papilloedema → raised ICP / tumour / abscess (see brain tumour, brain abscess)
🟣Migraine
  • Episodic, often unilateral throbbing, 4–72 h, with nausea, photophobia / phonophobia, worse on activity
  • ± aura (visual zig-zags / scotoma, spreading over 5–60 min then resolving); identifiable triggers
  • Acute: triptan + NSAID; prophylaxis (propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate) if frequent (see primary headaches)
🟢Tension-type & medication-overuse
  • Tension-type: bilateral, band-like, pressing, mild–moderate, no nausea, not aggravated by activity
  • Medication-overuse headache: chronic daily headache with regular analgesic / triptan overuse — treat by withdrawal
  • Reassurance, simple analgesia, address triggers / stress; limit acute medication days
🔵Cluster & other TACs / neuralgia
  • Cluster headache: severe unilateral orbital / temporal pain, 15–180 min, in bouts, often nocturnal; the patient is restless / agitated
  • Autonomic features: ipsilateral lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, ptosis / miosis (partial Horner’s); acute Rx high-flow O₂ + SC sumatriptan
  • Trigeminal neuralgia: paroxysmal electric-shock facial pain in a trigeminal division, trigger zones — carbamazepine
🩺Assess & investigate
  • Examine: BP, temperature, fundoscopy (papilloedema), neck stiffness, focal neurology, temporal arteries
  • Bloods: ESR / CRP (GCA); CT head for thunderclap / focal signs, LP after CT for SAH (xanthochromia) and meningitis
  • MRI / MR venography for CVST or posterior-fossa / progressive headache; check carbon monoxide if household / seasonal
Headache is a screening problem first: run the red flags — thunderclap (SAH), fever + meningism (meningitis), >50 + scalp tenderness (GCA), progressive + papilloedema (raised ICP / tumour). Only once these are excluded do you pattern-match the primary headache by site, duration and associated features.

NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo:
“Dizziness” is a bucket word — the first job is to classify it: vertigo (an illusion of movement / spinning → vestibular), presyncope (light-headed, about to faint → cardiovascular), disequilibrium (unsteadiness on walking → cerebellar / sensory / drugs) or psychogenic. For true vertigo, the key split is peripheral (labyrinth / vestibular nerve — usually benign) vs central (brainstem / cerebellum). The finals skill is not missing a central cause — a posterior circulation stroke — using the HINTS exam.
🚨In acute persistent vertigo, features that point to a central cause (posterior circulation stroke) are a NORMAL head impulse test, direction-changing or vertical nystagmus, a skew deviation, other brainstem / cerebellar signs (diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia, weakness) or inability to stand / walk unaided — the HINTS exam is more sensitive than early MRI (see stroke / TIA). Sudden headache / neck pain with vertigo suggests vertebral artery dissection. Do not label it “peripheral” without excluding these.

1Recognise & classify
🔍Classify the “dizziness”
  • Vertigo: illusion of movement / spinning → vestibular (then peripheral vs central)
  • Presyncope: light-headed, about to black out → cardiovascular (arrhythmia, orthostatic), anaemia, hypoglycaemia (see syncope / pre-syncope)
  • Disequilibrium: unsteadiness only on standing / walking → cerebellar, sensory ataxia, Parkinsonism, polypharmacy
🚩Central red flags (HINTS)
  • Acute persistent vertigo with a NORMAL head impulse test, direction-changing / vertical nystagmus or skew deviation → central (INFARCT) — HINTS is only valid in active vertigo with spontaneous nystagmus
  • Other brainstem / cerebellar signs (diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia, weakness) or cannot walk unaided → posterior circulation stroke (see stroke / TIA, ataxia)
  • Sudden headache / neck pain → vertebral artery dissection; consider vascular risk factors
🌀Peripheral vertigo
  • BPPV: brief (<1 min) positional vertigo on head turning / lying — Dix-Hallpike +, treat with Epley (see BPPV)
  • Vestibular neuritis: acute prolonged (days) severe vertigo, no hearing loss; labyrinthitis = the same + hearing loss / tinnitus (see vertigo & balance disorders) — but new acute hearing loss + vertigo can rarely be an AICA (labyrinthine) infarct
  • Ménière’s: episodic vertigo (20 min–hours) + fluctuating SNHL + tinnitus + aural fullness (see Ménière’s); acoustic neuroma: gradual unilateral SNHL + tinnitus
🧭Central vertigo
  • Posterior circulation stroke / TIA or cerebellar stroke — the must-not-miss cause (see stroke / TIA)
  • Vestibular migraine: vertigo with migrainous features (photophobia, headache, aura) — a common central cause
  • Multiple sclerosis (esp. young, other CNS episodes — see multiple sclerosis) and posterior-fossa tumours
💓Presyncope & disequilibrium
  • Cardiovascular: arrhythmia / heart block (see bradycardia / heart block), orthostatic hypotension (drugs, dehydration, autonomic)
  • Systemic: anaemia (see anaemia), hypoglycaemia (see hypoglycaemia)
  • Disequilibrium in the elderly is often multifactorial (vision, proprioception, cerebellar, drugs) — a falls risk (see falls assessment)
🩺Assess & investigate
  • Bedside: Dix-Hallpike (BPPV), HINTS (acute vestibular syndrome), lying-standing BP, otoscopy + Weber / Rinne, gait & full neuro exam
  • Presyncope: ECG, lying-standing BP, FBC / glucose; vertigo with central signs → MRI brain (posterior fossa)
  • Treat the cause: Epley for BPPV; short-course vestibular sedative (e.g. prochlorperazine) for acute peripheral only; betahistine for Ménière’s
Start by classifying the dizziness — vertigo vs presyncope vs disequilibrium. For vertigo, decide peripheral vs central: brief positional = BPPV; prolonged with hearing loss = labyrinthitis / Ménière’s; and any normal head impulse test, vertical / direction-changing nystagmus, skew or other neuro signs = central stroke until proven otherwise.

NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness:
Weakness means a genuine loss of power — first separate it from fatigue, pain-limited or functional weakness (a positive Hoover’s sign suggests functional). Then localise the lesion using tone, reflexes, wasting, fasciculations and the plantars: is it upper motor neuron (UMN), lower motor neuron (LMN), neuromuscular junction (NMJ) or muscle? Add the distribution (hemiparesis, paraparesis, quadriparesis, monoparesis, proximal vs distal). Localisation drives the differential and separates a benign myopathy from a stroke or cord compression.
🚨Acute focal weakness → stroke — FAST, urgent CT and thrombolysis / thrombectomy window (see stroke / TIA). Bilateral leg weakness with a sensory level + spastic (UMN) legs + bladder / bowel → cord compression; saddle anaesthesia + flaccid areflexic legs + retention → cauda equina — emergency MRI (see spinal cord compression, cauda equina). Rapidly ascending weakness with areflexia → Guillain-Barré; fatigable bulbar / respiratory weakness → myasthenic crisis — both need FVC monitoring (oxygen saturation falls late).

1Recognise & classify
🔍Confirm & localise
  • UMN: increased tone / spasticity, hyperreflexia, upgoing plantars, clonus, no wasting; pyramidal-pattern weakness
  • LMN: reduced tone, wasting, fasciculations, hyporeflexia, downgoing / absent plantars (see fasciculations)
  • NMJ: fatigable weakness, normal reflexes / sensation; Muscle: proximal symmetrical weakness, normal reflexes, no sensory loss
🚩Acute emergencies
  • Acute focal weakness → stroke (FAST, CT, thrombolysis window) (see stroke / TIA)
  • Sensory level + spastic legs → cord compression; saddle anaesthesia + flaccid legs + retention → cauda equina — emergency MRI (see cord compression, cauda equina)
  • Ascending flaccid weakness + areflexia (GBS) or fatigable bulbar / respiratory (myasthenic crisis) → monitor FVC (see Guillain-Barré, myasthenia)
🧠UMN causes
  • Brain: stroke (contralateral hemiparesis), tumour, MS demyelination (see stroke / TIA, multiple sclerosis)
  • Spinal cord: compression, transverse myelitis, MS → para- / quadriparesis with a sensory level (see spinal cord disorders)
  • Motor neurone disease: mixed UMN + LMN signs, no sensory loss (see motor neurone disease)
🔌LMN / nerve causes
  • Radiculopathy (root — myotomal weakness + dermatomal sensory loss, see radiculopathies); plexopathy
  • Peripheral neuropathy: distal symmetrical (“glove & stocking”) or a mononeuropathy (see peripheral nerve palsies)
  • Anterior horn cell: MND, (polio); facial (LMN) weakness — Bell’s palsy (see facial weakness)
🔋NMJ & muscle
  • Myasthenia gravis: fatigable weakness, ptosis, diplopia, bulbar symptoms (anti-AChR); Lambert-Eaton: improves with use, paraneoplastic (see neuromuscular junction disorders)
  • Myopathy: proximal symmetrical weakness — inflammatory (poly / dermatomyositis, see connective tissue disease), endocrine (thyroid, Cushing’s / steroids), drugs (statins)
  • Inherited dystrophies (e.g. Duchenne / Becker, see muscular dystrophies) — also proximal, high CK
🩺Assess & investigate
  • Grade power (MRC 0–5); map tone, reflexes, plantars, wasting, fasciculations, sensation and distribution
  • Imaging: CT / MRI brain (stroke / UMN), MRI spine (cord / cauda equina); NCS / EMG (LMN, NMJ, myopathy)
  • Bloods: CK (myopathy), TFTs, glucose; anti-AChR / MuSK (MG); LP for GBS (albuminocytological dissociation); FVC if neuromuscular (see MSK muscle weakness)
First confirm it is true weakness, then localise: UMN (spastic, brisk reflexes, upgoing plantars) vs LMN (wasting, fasciculations, absent reflexes) vs NMJ (fatigable) vs muscle (proximal, symmetric). Add the distribution — hemiparesis points to the brain, paraparesis to the cord, proximal-symmetric to muscle, ascending-flaccid to GBS. Time course helps too: sudden = vascular, hours–days = inflammatory (GBS), weeks = compressive, chronic = myopathy.

NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance:
Sensory disturbance — numbness / loss, paraesthesia (tingling) or dysaesthesia (unpleasant / painful) — is localised by the pattern of loss and which modalities are affected. Two pathways: the dorsal columns (vibration, proprioception, fine touch) and the spinothalamic tract (pain, temperature). Loss of one set with sparing of the other — dissociated sensory loss — localises to the cord. Otherwise the shape sorts it: a single nerve, a dermatome, a glove-and-stocking distribution, a sensory level, or a hemisensory pattern (thalamic / cortical).
🚨A sensory level with leg weakness and bladder / bowel dysfunction → cord compression — emergency MRI (see cord compression). Saddle anaesthesia with urinary retention → cauda equina (see cauda equina). Acute hemisensory loss → stroke (see stroke / TIA). Rapidly ascending sensory & motor loss with areflexia → Guillain-Barré. Sensory symptoms that seem “non-anatomical” still deserve a careful map before being called functional.

1Recognise & classify
🔍Characterise & the two pathways
  • Type: numbness / loss, paraesthesia (tingling — see paraesthesia & numbness) or dysaesthesia (painful)
  • Dorsal columns: vibration, proprioception, fine touch (ascend ipsilaterally, decussate in the medulla)
  • Spinothalamic: pain & temperature (decussate within 1–2 segments, ascend contralaterally) — loss of one set = dissociated (cord)
🚩Red flags
  • Sensory level + leg weakness + bladder / bowel → cord compression — emergency MRI (see cord compression)
  • Saddle anaesthesia + retention → cauda equina (see cauda equina); acute hemisensory loss → stroke (see stroke / TIA)
  • Rapidly ascending sensory & motor loss with areflexia → Guillain-Barré
🔌Peripheral patterns
  • Mononeuropathy: loss in one nerve’s territory (e.g. median → carpal tunnel, see Tinel’s / Phalen’s, peripheral nerve palsies; ulnar → little / ulnar-half ring; meralgia paraesthetica → anterolateral thigh)
  • Polyneuropathy: distal symmetrical “glove & stocking” (length-dependent) — diabetes (see diabetic neuropathy), alcohol, B12, drugs, CKD; hereditary (see Charcot-Marie-Tooth)
  • Radiculopathy: dermatomal loss + radicular pain + myotomal weakness — anchors: C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus, L4 medial malleolus, L5 big toe, S1 lateral foot (see radiculopathies)
🎗️Cord syndromes
  • Sensory level (loss below a horizontal level) → cord compression, transverse myelitis, MS (see spinal cord disorders, multiple sclerosis)
  • Brown-Séquard (hemicord): ipsilateral dorsal-column loss + UMN weakness, contralateral pain / temperature loss
  • Syringomyelia: “cape” dissociated loss (pain / temp over arms, dorsal columns spared); SACD (B12): dorsal columns + upgoing plantars with absent ankle jerks; anterior cord: pain / temp + motor lost, dorsal columns spared (see B12 / anaemia)
🧠Central (brainstem / thalamus / cortex)
  • Brainstem: crossed sensory loss — ipsilateral face, contralateral body (e.g. lateral medullary / Wallenberg)
  • Thalamus: contralateral hemisensory loss (all modalities) ± thalamic pain (Déjerine-Roussy)
  • Parietal cortex: cortical sensory loss — impaired two-point discrimination, stereognosis, sensory inattention, with primary modalities relatively preserved
🩺Assess & investigate
  • Map it: test light touch, pinprick (spinothalamic), vibration & proprioception (dorsal columns; a positive Romberg = sensory ataxia); define the pattern and any sensory level
  • Peripheral → nerve conduction studies, glucose / HbA1c, B12, TFTs, U&E; root / cord → MRI spine
  • Central / hemisensory → MRI brain (see weakness for the motor counterpart)
Localise sensory loss by its shape and modalities: a single nerve or dermatome = peripheral / root; glove-and-stocking = polyneuropathy; a sensory level or dissociated loss = cord; a hemisensory pattern = thalamic / cortical; and crossed (face vs body) = brainstem.

NEUROLOGICAL__Tremor:
Tremor is a rhythmic oscillation — the diagnosis turns on when it happens. Classify by activation: a rest tremor (present at rest, eases on movement) is Parkinsonian; a postural tremor (on holding the arms out) is enhanced physiological or essential; and an intention tremor (worsening as the finger nears a target) is cerebellar. Then add amplitude, frequency, symmetry and the associated features — bradykinesia, thyroid signs, alcohol response or a family history — to name the cause. (For the wider picture see movement disorders.)
🚨Do not miss the treatable / dangerous causes. Young patient with tremor + liver or psychiatric disease → screen for Wilson’s disease (treatable, see Wilson’s). Coarse tremor + confusion / GI upset on lithium → lithium toxicity (see drug toxicity). Fine fast tremor + weight loss, sweating, tachycardia → thyrotoxicosis (see hyperthyroidism). Tremor + agitation / hallucinations after stopping alcohol → withdrawal / delirium tremens (see alcohol withdrawal).

1Recognise & classify
🔍Classify by activation
  • Rest tremor: present at rest, reduced by movement; slow (4–6 Hz), “pill-rolling” → Parkinsonism
  • Postural tremor: on holding the arms outstretched → enhanced physiological or essential tremor
  • Intention tremor: worsens approaching a target (finger-nose), with past-pointing → cerebellar (see ataxia)
🚩Don’t-miss / treatable
  • Young + tremor + liver / psychiatric disease → Wilson’s disease (Kayser-Fleischer rings, low caeruloplasmin) — treatable (see Wilson’s)
  • Coarse tremor + confusion / vomiting / diarrhoea on lithium → lithium toxicity (see drug toxicity)
  • Fine fast tremor + thyrotoxic features → hyperthyroidism (see hyperthyroidism); alcohol-withdrawal tremor risks delirium tremens (see alcohol withdrawal)
🟣Rest tremor — Parkinsonism
  • Asymmetric slow pill-rolling rest tremor with bradykinesia and rigidity → Parkinson’s disease (see Parkinson’s disease)
  • Drug-induced parkinsonism: often more symmetric — antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine
  • Contrast the “liver flap” (asterixis) — a loss of tone, not a true tremor (see asterixis)
🟢Postural — essential & physiological
  • Essential tremor: bilateral, symmetric postural / action tremor; improves with alcohol, positive family history; affects hands, head (titubation) and voice — Rx propranolol (avoid in asthma; use primidone) (see essential tremor)
  • Enhanced physiological tremor: fine, fast — anxiety (see anxiety), caffeine, thyrotoxicosis, drugs (salbutamol, lithium, valproate), hypoglycaemia
  • A normal low-amplitude physiological tremor is present in everyone
🔵Intention & other patterns
  • Intention (cerebellar) tremor: worsens toward the target + dysmetria / past-pointing — MS (see multiple sclerosis), stroke, alcohol, posterior-fossa tumour
  • Wilson’s: coarse proximal “wing-beating” tremor in a young patient (see Wilson’s)
  • Functional (psychogenic) tremor: variable, distractible, changes with attention / entrainment
🩺Assess & investigate
  • Examine at rest, with arms outstretched and on finger-nose; note symmetry, frequency and associated signs (bradykinesia, cerebellar, thyroid)
  • Bloods: TFTs; copper studies (caeruloplasmin) if young; drug / alcohol history; glucose
  • Mostly a clinical diagnosis; DaTscan can separate Parkinsonian from essential tremor; MRI for a cerebellar cause
When does it happen? Rest tremor (eased by movement) = Parkinsonism; postural (arms out) = essential / physiological; intention (worse toward a target) = cerebellar. Then let the company decide: bradykinesia (Parkinson’s), alcohol response + family history (essential), thyroid / drug features (physiological).

NEUROLOGICAL__Ataxia:
Ataxia is incoordination out of proportion to weakness — a failure of smooth, accurate movement. The first question is where the lesion is. Cerebellar ataxia gives clumsy limbs, a wide-based gait and DANISH signs; sensory ataxia comes from loss of proprioception (dorsal columns / peripheral nerve) and is much worse with the eyes shut; vestibular ataxia is a veering gait with vertigo. The bedside divider is Romberg’s test (see Romberg’s): positive (falls only with eyes closed) points to a sensory cause, while a cerebellar patient is unsteady with eyes open or shut.
🚨Acute ataxia is a stroke until proven otherwise. Sudden ataxia + headache / vomiting / reduced consciousness → cerebellar stroke (posterior fossa — risk of brainstem compression & obstructive hydrocephalus; needs urgent imaging, see stroke). Ataxia + confusion + eye-movement signs, especially with alcohol or vomiting → Wernicke’s encephalopathy — give IV thiamine before any glucose (see Wernicke’s). Ataxia with a headache worse on lying / straining raises a posterior-fossa mass (see tumour).

1Recognise & localise
🔍Localise: cerebellar vs sensory vs vestibular
  • Cerebellar: intention tremor, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesis, scanning speech, nystagmus; wide-based gait; Romberg negative
  • Sensory: loss of joint-position & vibration sense, Romberg positive, much worse in the dark; high-stepping / stamping gait, pseudoathetosis
  • Vestibular: veering / falling to one side with vertigo (see vertigo) and nystagmus — no limb ataxia
🚩Acute — don’t miss
  • Cerebellar stroke: sudden ataxia + headache / vomiting ± reduced GCS — posterior fossa risks coning & hydrocephalus; urgent CT/MRI (see stroke / TIA)
  • Wernicke’s encephalopathy: ataxia + confusion + ophthalmoplegia / nystagmus — give IV thiamine before glucose (see Wernicke’s)
  • Posterior-fossa mass or first presentation of MS can also present acutely (see brain tumours, MS)
🔵Cerebellar syndrome (DANISH)
  • Dysdiadochokinesis, Ataxia, Nystagmus, Intention tremor (see tremor), Scanning speech, Hypotonia / heel-shin dysmetria
  • Hemisphere lesion → ipsilateral limb ataxia; vermis / midline lesion → truncal & gait ataxia
  • Causes: stroke, MS (see multiple sclerosis), tumour, alcohol, paraneoplastic
🟢Sensory ataxia (dorsal columns)
  • Romberg positive — unsteadiness that appears / worsens when the eyes close; loss of vibration & joint-position sense
  • B12 deficiency → subacute combined degeneration (dorsal columns + pyramidal signs; see B12 deficiency); also diabetic sensory neuropathy
  • Tabes dorsalis (tertiary syphilis) — classic sensory ataxia with lightning pains & Argyll Robertson pupils
🟡Chronic, inherited & toxic
  • Alcohol → midline (vermis) degeneration — gait ataxia (see alcohol); phenytoin toxicity → ataxia + nystagmus (see phenytoin)
  • Friedreich’s ataxia: young, progressive; absent reflexes with extensor plantars, pes cavus, scoliosis, HOCM, diabetes
  • Also paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration, hypothyroidism, and gluten (coeliac) ataxia (see coeliac)
🩺Assess & investigate
  • Gait (wide-based / heel-toe), finger-nose (dysmetria + intention tremor), heel-shin, dysdiadochokinesis, eye movements (nystagmus), speech; Romberg to split sensory from cerebellar
  • Examine proprioception & vibration, reflexes and plantars; check drug / alcohol history and any red-flag headache
  • MRI brain (posterior fossa) for cerebellar signs; B12, glucose / HbA1c, TFTs, phenytoin level; consider paraneoplastic screen & genetics
Romberg splits the room. A patient who is steady with eyes open but falls when they close is sensory (they were using vision to compensate for lost proprioception). A patient who is unsteady whether the eyes are open or shut is cerebellar — Romberg is negative, and that is a common exam trap.

NEUROLOGICAL__Confusion / Delirium:
Confusion is a symptom, not a diagnosis — the first job is to place it. Delirium is acute, fluctuating, and defined by inattention with an altered level of consciousness; it is common, dangerous and reversible, so it is the one to catch (see delirium). Dementia is chronic and progressive with a clear consciousness (see dementia); psychosis and depression are the other mimics. Delirium comes in three flavours — hyperactive (agitated), hypoactive (drowsy, withdrawn — easily missed and worse prognosis) and mixed. Beware too the patient whose “confusion” is really a dysphasia (see dysphasia).
🚨Exclude the immediately reversible / dangerous causes first. Check the glucose in every confused patient — hypoglycaemia is instantly treatable (see hypoglycaemia). Then hypoxia, sepsis / meningitis (see sepsis, meningitis), raised ICP / head injury (a subdural in the elderly or anticoagulated, see intracranial haemorrhage), Wernicke’s (give thiamine, see Wernicke’s) and drug toxicity or withdrawal (opioids, benzodiazepines, alcohol → delirium tremens, see drug / alcohol).

1Recognise & screen
🔍Recognise & screen
  • Acute onset + fluctuating course + inattention ± altered consciousness / disorganised thinking = delirium
  • Screen with the 4AT or CAM; test attention (e.g. months of the year backwards)
  • Hyperactive (agitated, hallucinating) vs hypoactive (drowsy, quiet — easily missed, worse outcome) vs mixed
🚩Immediately reversible / dangerous
  • Check glucose (hypoglycaemia, see hypoglycaemia) and oxygen saturations (hypoxia) in every confused patient
  • Sepsis / meningitis (see sepsis, meningitis); Wernicke’s → give thiamine (see Wernicke’s)
  • Raised ICP / head injury — subdural in the elderly / anticoagulated (see intracranial haemorrhage); drug toxicity or withdrawal (opioids, benzos, alcohol)
🟢Find the precipitant (PINCH ME)
  • Pain · Infection (UTI, chest, see UTI) · Nutrition · Constipation (see constipation) · Hydration (dehydration)
  • Medication (opioids, anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, steroids — see drug causes) · Environment / electrolytes
  • Urinary retention (see retention) and constipation are classic, easily reversed precipitants in the elderly
🔵Delirium vs dementia vs depression
  • Delirium: acute, fluctuating, inattentive, clouded consciousness, reversible
  • Dementia: chronic, progressive, clear consciousness, memory-led (see dementia) — but delirium is often superimposed on dementia
  • Depression (pseudodementia): low mood, poor effort / “don’t know” answers (see depression); psychosis has fixed delusions with clear consciousness (see psychosis)
🟡Special contexts
  • Post-operative delirium — very common in the elderly (anaesthetic, pain, opioids, infection, immobility)
  • Alcohol withdrawal → tremor, then delirium tremens (agitation, hallucinations, autonomic instability, seizures) — treat with benzodiazepines + thiamine (see alcohol withdrawal)
  • Anticholinergic burden (oxybutynin, amitriptyline, antihistamines) and opioids are frequent drug culprits (see drug toxicity)
🩺Assess & investigate
  • Confusion screen: FBC, U&E, glucose, calcium, LFTs, TFTs, CRP; urine culture (dipstick unreliable >65), blood cultures, CXR, ECG; CT head if focal signs, head injury, anticoagulated or no cause found
  • Collateral history & baseline cognition; AMTS / 4AT; full medication review (stop the culprit)
  • Treat the cause; non-pharmacological measures first (orientation, sleep, hydration, mobilise); if severe distress, short-term low-dose haloperidol (avoid in Parkinson’s / Lewy body — use lorazepam)
Hypoactive delirium is the trap. The quiet, drowsy, withdrawn patient is missed far more often than the agitated one — yet carries a worse prognosis. If you suspect it, formally test attention (months backwards, serial sevens): inattention is the hallmark that separates delirium from a settled dementia.

NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousness / Co:
Consciousness needs both arousal (the brainstem reticular activating system) and awareness (the cortex) — so coma follows either a brainstem lesion or widespread cortical dysfunction. Quantify depth with the GCS (eye / verbal / motor, out of 15) or AVPU; a GCS of 8 or less means the patient cannot protect the airway. The great divide is structural (a focal mass, bleed or brainstem lesion — expect focal / asymmetrical signs) versus diffuse metabolic, toxic or hypoxic causes (expect symmetrical signs with preserved pupil reflexes). This is a lower level of the same axis as confusion / delirium.
🚨Resuscitate first: A–E, and if GCS ≤8 protect the airway. Give the reversibles at once — glucose for hypoglycaemia (“Don’t Ever Forget Glucose”, see hypoglycaemia), naloxone for opioid toxicity (see opioid overdose) and thiamine for possible Wernicke’s (see Wernicke’s). Look for coning: a fixed, dilated pupil with falling GCS and a Cushing response (hypertension + bradycardia) means raised ICP — urgent CT and neurosurgery (see raised ICP). Don’t forget meningitis / encephalitis and non-convulsive status.

1Resuscitate & localise
🔍Resuscitate & quantify
  • A–E first; if GCS ≤8 the airway is unsafe — get anaesthetic / critical-care help to intubate
  • Score the GCS (best eye /4, verbal /5, motor /6) and reassess the trend; check pupils (see abnormal pupils), temperature and a capillary glucose
  • Get a collateral history — onset, drugs, trauma, diabetes, epilepsy, alcohol
🚩Give the reversibles now
  • Glucose for hypoglycaemia (see hypoglycaemia) — give thiamine first if malnourished / alcohol (Wernicke’s, see Wernicke’s)
  • Naloxone for opioid toxicity (pinpoint pupils, low respiratory rate, see opioid overdose)
  • Correct hypoxia / hypercapnia (see respiratory failure) and treat sepsis (see sepsis)
🔵Structural vs metabolic
  • Structural (mass, bleed, brainstem stroke): focal / asymmetrical signs, abnormal / unequal pupils, lateralising weakness (see intracranial haemorrhage, stroke)
  • Metabolic / toxic: symmetrical, preserved pupil light reflexes (even when deep), fluctuating level, myoclonus / asterixis (see liver flap)
  • Pupils are the key discriminator — asymmetry until proven otherwise is structural
🟢Toxic & metabolic patterns
  • Opioids: pinpoint pupils + low RR → naloxone; benzodiazepines / alcohol: sedation with normal pupils
  • TCA overdose (wide QRS, seizures), salicylate (tachypnoea, tinnitus), CO poisoning (headache, house fire / faulty heater), see toxicology
  • DKA / HHS (Kussmaul breathing, ketones, see DKA), uraemia, hyponatraemia, hepatic encephalopathy, hypercapnia
🟡Raised ICP & coning
  • Falling GCS + a fixed, dilated pupil (third-nerve / uncal herniation) is a neurosurgical emergency (see raised ICP, and the signs of raised ICP)
  • Cushing response: hypertension + bradycardia ± irregular breathing — a late, ominous sign
  • Urgent CT head; temporise with head-up 30°, osmotic therapy (mannitol / hypertonic saline) and airway control; call neurosurgery
🩺Assess & investigate
  • Brainstem reflexes: pupillary light, corneal, gag / cough, and oculocephalic (“doll’s eyes”) responses; watch for subtle seizure activity (see seizures)
  • Bloods: glucose, U&E, LFTs, calcium, ABG, FBC / CRP, toxicology (paracetamol / salicylate), ammonia; blood cultures if septic
  • CT head early; LP if meningitis / encephalitis suspected (see meningitis, after CT); EEG for non-convulsive status (see status epilepticus)
Pupils split structural from metabolic. Most metabolic and toxic comas spare the pupillary light reflex (the classic exception is opioids — pinpoint but reactive). So asymmetrical or fixed pupils point to a structural lesion and demand an urgent CT, while symmetrical reactive pupils in a deeply unconscious patient favour a metabolic / toxic cause.

NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures:
A seizure is a paroxysm of abnormal, synchronous cortical electrical activity. First classify it: a focal seizure starts in one region — with retained or impaired awareness, ± motor signs or automatisms, and it may evolve to a bilateral tonic-clonic seizure; a generalised seizure involves both hemispheres from the outset (tonic-clonic, absence, myoclonic, tonic, atonic). Then make the diagnosis that matters most: an epileptic seizure vs its mimics — syncope (see transient LOC), a non-epileptic attack, or hypoglycaemia. Epilepsy is a tendency to recurrent, unprovoked seizures (see epilepsy) — a single provoked fit is not epilepsy.
🚨Status epilepticus — a seizure lasting ≥5 minutes or repeated fits without recovery — is an emergency: ABC, oxygen, glucose and a timed benzodiazepine escalation (see status epilepticus). In pregnancy / postpartum a seizure is eclampsia until proven otherwise → magnesium sulfate (see eclampsia). Screen for hypoglycaemia (see hypoglycaemia) and hyponatraemia (see electrolytes), CNS infection (fever / meningism, see meningitis / encephalitis) and head injury. A new focal seizure in an adult is a structural lesion (tumour / bleed, see brain tumour) until MRI proves otherwise.

NEUROLOGICAL__Transient Loss of Consciou:
Transient loss of consciousness (TLoC) is a brief, self-limiting loss of consciousness with complete spontaneous recovery. Sort it into three buckets: syncope (transient global cerebral hypoperfusion — reflex/vasovagal, orthostatic or cardiac, see syncope), an epileptic seizure (see seizures), or a psychogenic attack. The two tests that carry the whole assessment are the eyewitness history and a 12-lead ECG. First make sure it really was TLoC — exclude hypoglycaemia (see hypoglycaemia), intoxication and head trauma.
🚨Cardiac syncope is the one that kills. Treat TLoC as cardiac — and refer / admit — if there is any of: syncope on exertion or while lying flat, palpitations just before, no prodrome (sudden, “lights-out”), a family history of sudden cardiac death <40 or inherited channelopathy, known structural heart disease (e.g. aortic stenosis, see valvular disease; HCM, see cardiomyopathy), or an abnormal ECG (long QT, Brugada, complete heart block / bifascicular block, see heart block; VT / WPW, see tachyarrhythmia).

NEUROLOGICAL__Visual Field Defects:
The field defect localises the lesion along the visual pathway. A monocular loss is pre-chiasmal (retina or optic nerve); a bitemporal hemianopia is the chiasm; a homonymous hemianopia or quadrantanopia is retrochiasmal (optic tract, radiation or cortex). The further back the lesion, the more congruous the defect — and an occipital (cortical) lesion classically spares the macula. Test each eye separately, check for a relative afferent pupillary defect (see abnormal pupils) and map the field: the pattern is the diagnosis.
🚨Sudden painless monocular loss is a “stroke of the eye” — central retinal artery occlusion (see CRAO); always exclude giant cell arteritis (jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, raised ESR → high-dose steroids to save the other eye, see GCA). Amaurosis fugax is a TIA warning. A new homonymous hemianopia is a stroke until proven otherwise (see stroke). A bitemporal defect with sudden headache & ophthalmoplegia is pituitary apoplexy (see pituitary); and flashes, floaters & a curtain signal retinal detachment (see detachment).

NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia:
Diplopia divides at the first question: monocular or binocular? Cover one eye. Monocular diplopia persists with the other eye covered — it is an ocular / refractive problem (cataract, astigmatism, dry eye, dislocated lens) and reassuring. Binocular diplopia disappears when either eye is covered — the eyes are misaligned, and the cause lies in a cranial nerve (III, IV, VI), the neuromuscular junction, an extraocular muscle / orbit, or the brainstem. That is where the danger sits. Work out which movement fails and check the pupil (see abnormal pupils).
🚨A painful third-nerve palsy with a fixed, dilated pupil is a posterior communicating artery aneurysm until proven otherwise — urgent CT / CT angiography, risk of subarachnoid haemorrhage (see aneurysm / haemorrhage). Diplopia with other cranial nerves or brainstem signs suggests a stroke (see stroke) or cavernous sinus lesion. Fatigable, variable diplopia with ptosis is myasthenia — watch the bulbar / respiratory risk (see myasthenia). An isolated sixth-nerve palsy can be a false-localising sign of raised ICP, and painful ophthalmoplegia in the elderly may be giant cell arteritis (see GCA).

The pupil decides the third nerve. Parasympathetic fibres travel on the surface of CN III, so a compressive lesion (aneurysm) catches the pupil (fixed, dilated) — a surgical emergency — while a microvascular (diabetic) palsy spares the pupil. NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulbar Pals:
Bulbar and pseudobulbar palsy both disrupt the muscles of speech and swallowing (cranial nerves IX–XII), giving the same triad — dysarthria, dysphagia and dysphonia — but at different levels. Bulbar palsy is a lower motor neurone lesion of the medullary nuclei / nerves: a flaccid, wasted, fasciculating tongue, a normal or absent jaw jerk and nasal speech. Pseudobulbar palsy is an upper motor neurone lesion (bilateral corticobulbar tracts): a small, spastic, immobile tongue, a brisk jaw jerk, strangled “hot-potato” speech and emotional lability. The tongue and jaw jerk separate them (see dysarthria).
🚨An unsafe swallow is the emergency. Choking, wet voice or nasal regurgitation mean aspiration risk → keep the patient nil by mouth, get an urgent SALT assessment and protect nutrition (see dysphagia). A bulbar palsy with limb weakness may be Guillain-Barré or myasthenia — watch for respiratory failure and monitor the FVC (falling vital capacity, not the oxygen saturations, warns first; see Guillain-Barré, myasthenia). An acute bulbar palsy is a brainstem stroke (see stroke); bulbar-onset MND carries a poor prognosis (see MND).

1Recognise & localise
🔍Recognise the syndrome
  • The triad: dysarthria (slurred speech), dysphagia (choking, nasal regurgitation) and dysphonia (weak / nasal / strangled voice)
  • From dysfunction of cranial nerves IX (glossopharyngeal), X (vagus), XI (accessory) and XII (hypoglossal)
  • Decide the level: lower motor neurone (bulbar) vs upper motor neurone (pseudobulbar)
🚩Swallow & respiratory safety
  • Unsafe swallow (choking, wet voice, nasal regurgitation) → nil by mouth, urgent SALT & video-fluoroscopy; risk of aspiration pneumonia (see dysphagia)
  • Bulbar + limb weakness → Guillain-Barré or myasthenia; monitor FVC for respiratory failure (see Guillain-Barré, myasthenia)
  • Acute onset → brainstem stroke (see stroke); protect nutrition (NG / PEG feeding)
🟢Bulbar palsy (LMN)
  • Tongue: flaccid, wasted, fasciculating (see fasciculations); jaw jerk normal or absent; gag absent
  • Speech is nasal / quiet; palate moves poorly
  • Causes: MND (see MND), Guillain-Barré, myasthenia, brainstem infarct, syringobulbia, poliomyelitis
🔵Pseudobulbar palsy (UMN)
  • Tongue: small, spastic, immobile (no wasting or fasciculation); jaw jerk brisk; gag brisk
  • Speech is strangled / “hot-potato” (spastic); emotional lability (pathological crying / laughing)
  • Causes: bilateral strokes (see stroke), MS (see multiple sclerosis), MND, high brainstem lesions
🟡Distinguish them (& MND overlap)
  • Tongue: wasted & fasciculating (bulbar) vs small & spastic (pseudobulbar); jaw jerk: absent vs brisk
  • Speech: nasal (bulbar) vs strangled / spastic (pseudobulbar); affect: normal vs labile
  • MND can give a mixed picture — UMN and LMN signs together (e.g. brisk jaw jerk with a fasciculating tongue)
🩺Assess & investigate
  • Examine CN IX–XII: tongue (wasting / fasciculation / movement), palatal / gag reflex, jaw jerk, speech and the swallow
  • SALT assessment ± video-fluoroscopy; MRI brain / brainstem; EMG / nerve conduction (MND, GBS); anti-AChR (myasthenia); FVC
  • Address nutrition (NG / PEG) and aspiration prevention; look for limb UMN / LMN signs to unmask MND
The tongue and the jaw jerk decide it. A wasted, fasciculating tongue with an absent jaw jerk is bulbar (LMN); a small, spastic tongue with a brisk jaw jerk — especially with emotional lability — is pseudobulbar (UMN). Remember MND can show both at once.
